Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Working with Web Pages: HTML Parsing
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Working with Web Pages: HTML Parsing

Learn how HTML organizes content into tags, attributes, and a parse tree. Use BeautifulSoup to parse pages robustly and extract text and links for analysis.

Orientation

You'll see what makes HTML hierarchical, why regex often fails on nested markup, and how BeautifulSoup builds a navigable tree. Practical code examples guide you from raw HTML to a reliable extract of titles and links.

Explore Key Topics
HTML Structure
Tags, attributes, and element hierarchy form the parse tree you navigate.
Parsing Tools
BeautifulSoup sits on a parser and makes traversal and search simple and robust.
Extraction
Extract text with get_text() and attributes with get('name').
Visual concept
A page is a tree: parent elements contain children and siblings. Parsers build this tree so you can search reliably.
Element
<div class="cards">
Attribute
href, src, id, class
Parse Tree
Nodes connected as parent, child, and sibling relationships for traversal.
Key Takeaway

Use an HTML parser to create a resilient parse tree. Avoid regex for complex, nested documents.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical abilities that make web scraping reliable and maintainable. First, you will recognize H T M L structure: how tags, attributes, and element relationships form a tree. You will be able to inspect a page and identify which tags and attributes to target. Second, you will explain why regular expressions are a brittle choice for parsing H T M L: nested and malformed markup breaks simple patterns, while a parser understands structure. Third, you will install and use BeautifulSoup to build a parse tree and run searches with methods like find and find_all; you will be able to extract text and attribute values. Finally, you will navigate parse trees to find elements by tag, id, and class and avoid common mistakes such as forgetting the parser or using the reserved word class incorrectly. Each objective combines a description and a reason it matters, so you learn both the how and the why. These skills let you move from raw H T M L to structured data with confidence.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Learning Objectives — Practice

Practice & tooling

Inspect and choose targets
  • Use developer tools to find unique IDs or stable classes to target.
  • Prefer structural attributes over visual layout markers that change often.
  • Test selectors on several pages or items to ensure they are consistent.
Defensive parsing habits
  • Check for None before accessing attributes or text.
  • Handle missing attributes by using get('attr') and defaulting when needed.
  • Log unexpected structures and move on instead of failing fast in production scrapers.
Tip
When HTML is messy, install and use 'lxml' as the parser for better tolerance of malformed tags.
Key Takeaway

Combine inspection, defensive code, and an appropriate parser to build robust scrapers.

screens.title: HTML Structure: Tags, Attributes, and Hierarchy
screens.narratorSegment: H T M L is a markup language that expresses a document as a hierarchy of elements. Each element is a tag such as div, p, a, or img, and can contain attributes like id, class, href, or src which provide metadata or targets for code. When parsed, an H T M L document becomes a tree: elements are nodes that may be parents, children, or siblings. Parents contain child nodes, and sibling nodes share the same parent. This tree view matters because parsers operate by walking nodes rather than scanning raw text. A concrete example: a list of links is often constructed with a ul or ol element whose children are li elements, and each li contains an anchor tag with an href attribute. To extract the link targets you navigate to each li, find the a tag inside it, and read its href. A common misconception is to treat H T M L as flat text; that leads to fragile approaches. Inspect the DOM in your browser to verify nesting before coding. Takeaway: think in nodes and relationships, not lines of text.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › HTML Structure
Core Concept

Tags, attributes, and the DOM tree

Elements are nodes; attributes hold data. Treat the document as a tree for dependable traversal.

  • Tags define elements such as <p>, <a>, <div>.
  • Attributes like id and class provide hooks to find elements.
  • Parents contain children; siblings share a parent—use these relationships to navigate.
Key Takeaway

Design extraction logic around DOM relationships rather than text patterns.

Annotated example
<ul class="movies"> <li><a href="/m1">Movie A</a></li> <li><a href="/m2">Movie B</a></li> </ul> This structure shows a parent <ul> with child <li> elements, each containing an <a> tag whose href is the actual URL.
Extraction plan
Find the <ul>, iterate its <li> children, then read each <a>'s href attribute.
Common mistake
Searching the raw HTML string for 'href' produces false matches outside desired list items.

screens.title: Why Not Regular Expressions?
screens.narratorSegment: Many beginners reach for regular expressions because they are familiar and quick for simple text patterns. But H T M L is not a regular language in the formal sense; it is a nested, context-sensitive structure. Regular expressions match sequences of characters, not hierarchical relationships. As a result, a regex that works on a small, tidy fragment will often fail when the page changes: an extra attribute, different whitespace, or an added wrapper element can break the pattern. A concrete example is trying to extract the text of an anchor tag with a regex. If nested tags or unexpected attributes appear inside the anchor, the pattern will fail or capture unwanted content. Another common problem is malformed H T M L: real-world pages sometimes omit closing tags or nest elements incorrectly. Parsers like the ones behind BeautifulSoup are designed to build a tree even from imperfect H T M L and to provide robust search methods. The misconception to avoid is assuming text patterns are stable; instead, prefer a parser and target structural features like tags and attributes. Why Not Regular Expressions? means regular expressions break on nested structures and minor markup changes; html parsers handle structure and malformed markup gracefully.. In practical terms, the limits of regex when working with nested or malformed html. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Why Not Regular Expressions?
Comparison

Regex vs HTML Parser

  • Regex: matches text patterns, brittle to nesting and malformed tags.
  • Parser: builds a DOM-like tree and tolerates imperfect HTML.
  • Use parser methods to find elements by tag and attribute rather than searching strings.
Warning
If you find yourself writing complex regex for nested tags, switch to a parser — it will save time and prevent subtle bugs.
Fragile regex example (illustration)
A regex like: <a.*?href=\"(.*?)\".*?>(.*?)</a> can fail if inner markup contains tags or attributes change order.
Parser approach
Use BeautifulSoup's find_all('a') then for each anchor read get('href') and get_text() for robust results.
Key Takeaway

Choose tools that model the structure of your data. Parsers understand trees; regex does not.

A typical workflow is to fetch H T M L with a library such as urllib, decode it to a string, then pass it into BeautifulSoup. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Install & Parse
Process Flow

Install and create a BeautifulSoup object

Install beautifulsoup4, optionally lxml, fetch HTML, then parse.
pip install beautifulsoup4
# Optional for a faster parser:
pip install lxml

from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
import urllib.request

with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as response:
  html = response.read().decode('utf-8')

soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser')  # or 'lxml' if installed
print(soup.title.string)
Why parser choice matters
html.parser is built-in; lxml can handle malformed HTML more robustly.
Common mistake
Specifying 'lxml' without installing it will raise an import error.
Quick example
Create a BeautifulSoup object and print the page title using the built-in parser. This confirms parsing succeeded.
Key Takeaway

Install, fetch, decode, and then parse. Choose the parser for resilience against malformed pages.

screens.title: Finding Elements: find() and find_all()
screens.narratorSegment: BeautifulSoup provides simple, intuitive search methods. The find method returns the first matching element, while find_all returns a list of all matches. You can pass a tag name, or filters such as id or class_, to narrow results. For example, find('p') returns the first paragraph, while find_all('a') yields all anchor tags. Using class requires the special name class_ because class is a reserved word in Python. You can also pass dictionaries of attributes, C S S selectors, or even regular expressions to match tag names or attribute values for more advanced searches. A concrete example: to get all links inside list items, you might find all li tags then call find('a') on each. A common misconception is that find_all always returns elements in the same order; it will return elements in document order, which is usually what you want. Takeaway: prefer semantic filters like tag + attribute to keep code readable and robust. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › find() and find_all()
Definition

find and find_all explained

# First paragraph
first_p = soup.find('p')
print(first_p.get_text())

# All links
all_links = soup.find_all('a')
for link in all_links:
  print(link.get_text(), link.get('href'))

# Find by class (note class_)
stories = soup.find_all('p', class_='story')
Practical pattern
Use find to probe structure quickly. Use find_all when you need to collect many items for iteration and extraction.
Common mistake
Using class instead of class_ will raise a syntax error; remember the underscore when filtering by class.
Key Takeaway

find returns the first match, find_all returns a list. Use attribute filters for precise selection.

BeautifulSoup offers. get_text() which returns all the text inside an element and its children, with tags removed. Use. string when the element contains only a single text node;. string returns None if there are nested tags. To read attributes, call get with the attribute name, for example get('href') for a link target. A concrete example: after finding an anchor tag, call anchor. get_text() to get the visible link text and anchor. get('href') to get the URL. A common pitfall is relying on. string when the node contains inner tags—this returns None unexpectedly. Another practical note: strip results or handle whitespace because H T M L may contain newlines or extra spaces. Takeaway: prefer get_text() for robust extraction of visible text and use get('attr') for attributes, always checking for None to avoid runtime errors. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Extracting Text & Attributes

Methods to get text and attributes

# Text extraction
para = soup.find('p')
print(para.get_text())  # returns text from the element and children

# When element wraps plain text
span = soup.find('span', class_='course-title')
print(span.string)  # works only when span contains a single text node

# Attribute extraction
link = soup.find('a')
href = link.get('href')
print(href)
  • get_text() strips tags and returns combined visible text.
  • .string is fragile when elements have nested tags.
  • Use get('attr') to read attributes and check for None.
Example
For <span class="course-title">Python Programming</span> use find then .get_text() for the visible title.
Common mistake
Using element.string without checking for nested tags can yield None and cause attribute errors when you call strip() or similar methods.
Key Takeaway

Use get_text() for robust text; use get('attribute') and defensive checks for attributes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Dormouse Example

Sample code

from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

html_doc = """
<html><head><title>The Dormouse's story</title></head>
<body>
<p class="title"><b>The Dormouse's story</b></p>

<a href="http://example.com/elsie" class="sister" id="link1">Elsie</a>,
<a href="http://example.com/lacie" class="sister" id="link2">Lacie</a> and
<a href="http://example.com/tillie" class="sister" id="link3">Tillie</a>;
</p>

<p class="story">...</p>

soup = BeautifulSoup(html_doc, 'html.parser')

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Scrape Movie List

Task steps

  1. Fetch the HTML from the provided URL and decode it to a string.
  2. Create a BeautifulSoup object with 'html.parser' or 'lxml' as available.

screens.title: Selecting by ID, Class, and Attributes
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right selector is often the difference between a scraper that lasts and one that breaks. IDs are usually unique on a page, making them excellent targets when present. Classes may be shared among many elements; use class_ to search for elements by class. Attributes like data-* or specific href values can also be used in attribute dictionaries passed to find or find_all. When a selector is ambiguous, consider narrowing context: find the container element first then search within it. For example, locate a div with id 'main-content' and then call find_all('a') inside it to restrict results. A common misconception is to pick selectors only by visual appearance; these are more likely to change. Prefer structural or semantic attributes such as id, stable classes, or tag hierarchies that reflect content, not layout. Practical tip: test selectors on multiple pages or items to ensure consistency before automating scrapers. ID, class, and attribute selection

Use IDs for uniqueness, class_ for shared styles, and attribute dictionaries for custom filters.

screens.title: Handling Real-world HTML and Errors
screens.narratorSegment: Real-world H T M L is rarely perfect. Pages may omit closing tags, include unexpected nested elements, or omit attributes you expect. BeautifulSoup and its underlying parsers are forgiving: they attempt to rebuild a sensible tree even from imperfect markup. However, your code must be defensive. Always check whether a find returned None before calling methods on the result. Use get('attr') instead of direct attribute access to avoid KeyError-like behavior. Choose a parser that suits the data: the built-in html. parser is convenient, while lxml tends to be faster and more tolerant of broken H T M L. When debugging, print the repr of nodes or their partial H T M L to confirm what the parser returned. A misconception is that parser choice will fix every issue; it helps, but defensive code is still necessary. Finally, add small logging or counters to monitor how often expected elements are missing—this helps you decide if selectors need updating or if the page structure changed. Tolerating imperfect pages

Design scripts to handle missing attributes and malformed markup gracefully.
Defensive code pattern
link = item.find('a')
if link is None:
  continue
href = link.get('href')  # safe access
if href:
  process(href)
  • Check for None before accessing methods or attributes.
  • Use get to read attributes and provide defaults when appropriate.
  • Log unexpected counts to detect structural changes early.
Parser choice
Try html.parser first; install lxml if HTML is messy or you need speed.
Debugging tip
Print parts of the parse tree or node contents to verify your selectors return the expected nodes before extracting attributes.
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Debugging Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring mistakes students make when learning H T M L parsing. The first is using class instead of class_ when filtering by class attribute; because class is a reserved word in Python you must use class_. The second is forgetting to specify or install the parser you intend to use; specifying 'lxml' without installing lxml will raise an error. The third is relying on fragile selectors tied to styling. Debugging strategies include printing intermediate results: element counts, repr of found nodes, and the partial H T M L of a selected element to confirm its structure. Add try/except around network fetches to distinguish connectivity errors from parsing issues. For missing attributes, use get with None checks instead of indexing directly. If results differ from expectation, open the raw H T M L in an editor or the browser and compare the DOM to your selector assumptions. These small checks will shorten debugging time and make your scraping workflows more reliable. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn to transform raw H T M L into meaningful data. We start by understanding H T M L as a nested tree of tags and attributes, then explain why regular expressions are brittle for this job. Next, you'll install and use the BeautifulSoup library to build a parse tree that you can navigate with clear, resilient methods. You will see how to find elements by tag, class, and id, how to extract textual content, and how to pull attribute values like links and image sources. A simple example will take you from a downloaded H T M L string to a list of links and titles. This skill matters because web pages are a rich public source of data for analysis, research, and automation; parsing them reliably prevents fragile scripts that break after small layout changes. As you watch the code examples and try the hands-on activity, focus on identifying unique tags and attributes that survive small page changes. By the end you will be able to fetch a page, parse it, and extract the information you need in a way that is robust and maintainable. Ready to explore the structure that underlies every web page?

By the end of this chapter you will have four practical abilities that make web scraping reliable and maintainable. First, you will recognize H T M L structure: how tags, attributes, and element relationships form a tree. You will be able to inspect a page and identify which tags and attributes to target. Second, you will explain why regular expressions are a brittle choice for parsing H T M L: nested and malformed markup breaks simple patterns, while a parser understands structure. Third, you will install and use BeautifulSoup to build a parse tree and run searches with methods like find and find_all; you will be able to extract text and attribute values. Finally, you will navigate parse trees to find elements by tag, id, and class and avoid common mistakes such as forgetting the parser or using the reserved word class incorrectly. Each objective combines a description and a reason it matters, so you learn both the how and the why. These skills let you move from raw H T M L to structured data with confidence.

This second objectives slide focuses on how you will practice and what habits keep your parsers resilient. You will learn to inspect pages with developer tools to find stable tags and attributes, and to prefer IDs or unique classes when present. You will practice defensive parsing: verify elements exist before using them, handle missing attributes, and choose a parser like lxml when H T M L is messy. You will also adopt small debugging steps: print intermediate node counts, inspect element contents, and open the raw H T M L in an editor when results differ from expectations. These habits reduce runtime errors and maintenance time. For example, if a link attribute is missing on some items, your code should skip or log that case rather than crashing. Each habit supports the main objective: extract meaningful data reliably from real-world, imperfect web pages.

H T M L is a markup language that expresses a document as a hierarchy of elements. Each element is a tag such as div, p, a, or img, and can contain attributes like id, class, href, or src which provide metadata or targets for code. When parsed, an H T M L document becomes a tree: elements are nodes that may be parents, children, or siblings. Parents contain child nodes, and sibling nodes share the same parent. This tree view matters because parsers operate by walking nodes rather than scanning raw text. A concrete example: a list of links is often constructed with a ul or ol element whose children are li elements, and each li contains an anchor tag with an href attribute. To extract the link targets you navigate to each li, find the a tag inside it, and read its href. A common misconception is to treat H T M L as flat text; that leads to fragile approaches. Inspect the DOM in your browser to verify nesting before coding. Takeaway: think in nodes and relationships, not lines of text.

Many beginners reach for regular expressions because they are familiar and quick for simple text patterns. But H T M L is not a regular language in the formal sense; it is a nested, context-sensitive structure. Regular expressions match sequences of characters, not hierarchical relationships. As a result, a regex that works on a small, tidy fragment will often fail when the page changes: an extra attribute, different whitespace, or an added wrapper element can break the pattern. A concrete example is trying to extract the text of an anchor tag with a regex. If nested tags or unexpected attributes appear inside the anchor, the pattern will fail or capture unwanted content. Another common problem is malformed H T M L: real-world pages sometimes omit closing tags or nest elements incorrectly. Parsers like the ones behind BeautifulSoup are designed to build a tree even from imperfect H T M L and to provide robust search methods. The misconception to avoid is assuming text patterns are stable; instead, prefer a parser and target structural features like tags and attributes. Why Not Regular Expressions? means regular expressions break on nested structures and minor markup changes; html parsers handle structure and malformed markup gracefully.. In practical terms, the limits of regex when working with nested or malformed html. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Getting started with BeautifulSoup is straightforward. First, install the package using pip: this provides the BeautifulSoup A P I. Optionally install a faster and more forgiving parser like lxml; when H T M L is messy, lxml often yields better structure. In code, you create a BeautifulSoup object by passing the H T M L string and the parser name. This object builds the parse tree and offers methods for navigation and search. A typical workflow is to fetch H T M L with a library such as urllib, decode it to a string, then pass it into BeautifulSoup. Important practical points: always decode bytes to a string before parsing and choose a parser you installed. A common mistake is forgetting to install lxml but specifying it as the parser; this raises an error. The steps are simple but foundational: install, fetch, parse, then explore the tree. This is the setup that enables all downstream find and extraction methods. Installing BeautifulSoup and creating a parser means install beautifulsoup4, optionally lxml, fetch html, then create a beautifulsoup object with a chosen parser to build the parse tree.. In practical terms, pip install and creating a beautifulsoup object from html. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

BeautifulSoup provides simple, intuitive search methods. The find method returns the first matching element, while find_all returns a list of all matches. You can pass a tag name, or filters such as id or class_, to narrow results. For example, find('p') returns the first paragraph, while find_all('a') yields all anchor tags. Using class requires the special name class_ because class is a reserved word in Python. You can also pass dictionaries of attributes, C S S selectors, or even regular expressions to match tag names or attribute values for more advanced searches. A concrete example: to get all links inside list items, you might find all li tags then call find('a') on each. A common misconception is that find_all always returns elements in the same order; it will return elements in document order, which is usually what you want.
